paragraphs: In the upper ranks of life every duty is performed by deputies, as though duties could ever be waived; and the empty pleasures which the resulting idleness drives the rich to pursue look so tempting to the rank below that the crowds scrambling for wealth sacrifice everything to tread on their heels. The most sacred trusts are then treated as sinecures, because they were obtained through influence and sought only to let a man keep GOOD COMPANY. Women in particular all want to be ladies, which simply means having nothing to do but drift listlessly about, they hardly care where, for a purpose they cannot name.

But what, I may be asked, have women to do in society except to idle with an easy grace? Surely you would not condemn them all to suckle fools, and chronicle small beer! No. Women might certainly study the art of healing and be physicians as well as nurses. And decency seems to assign midwifery to them, though I am afraid that the word midwife in our dictionaries will soon give way to accoucheur, and that one proof of the sex’s former delicacy will be erased from the language.

They might also study politics, and ground their benevolence on the broadest foundation. For reading history will hardly be more useful than reading romances if it is read as mere biography, without noticing the character of the times, political improvements, the arts and so on; in short, if it is not regarded as the history of man, rather than of particular men who filled a niche in the temple of fame and then dropped into the black, rolling stream of time, which silently sweeps everything before it into the shapeless void called eternity. For can it be called a shape, “that shape hath none?”

They might likewise pursue business of various kinds, if they were educated in a more orderly way, and this might save many from common and legal prostitution. Women would not then marry for a living, as men accept government posts and neglect the duties those posts imply; nor would an attempt to earn their own living, a most praiseworthy attempt, sink them almost to the level of those poor abandoned creatures who live by prostitution. For are not milliners and dressmakers counted as the next class down? The few occupations open to women are far from liberal; they are menial. And when a better education enables them to take charge of children’s education as governesses, they are not treated like the tutors of sons; though even clergymen who serve as tutors are not always treated in a way likely to make them respected in the eyes of their pupils, to say nothing of their own private comfort. But since women educated as gentlewomen are never intended for the humiliating positions that necessity sometimes forces them to fill, these positions are regarded as a degradation; and anyone who needs to be told that nothing sharpens sensibility so painfully as such a fall in life knows little of the human heart.

Some of these women might be held back from marrying by a proper pride or delicacy, and others may not have been able to escape from servitude in this pitiful way. Is not that government, then, gravely defective, and heedless of the happiness of half its members, if it makes no provision for honest, independent women by encouraging them to fill respectable positions? But if their private virtue is to become a public benefit, they must have a civil existence in the state, whether married or single; otherwise we shall constantly see some worthy woman, whose sensibility has been made painfully acute by undeserved contempt, droop like “the lily broken down by a plough share.”

It is a sad truth; yet such are the blessed effects of civilization! The most respectable women are the most oppressed; and unless their understandings are far above the common run of understanding in both sexes, they must, from being treated as contemptible beings, become contemptible. How many women waste their lives away like this, a prey to discontent, who might have practised as physicians, run a farm, managed a shop and stood upright, supported by their own work, instead of hanging their heads, weighed down with the dew of sensibility that consumes the very beauty it at first gave lustre to! Indeed, I doubt whether pity and love are as closely related as poets pretend; for I have seldom seen much compassion aroused by the helplessness of women unless they were beautiful. Then, perhaps, pity was the gentle handmaid of love, or the forerunner of lust.

How much more respectable is the woman who earns her own bread by fulfilling any duty than the most accomplished beauty! Beauty, did I say? I am so conscious of the beauty of moral loveliness, or of that harmonious propriety which brings the passions of a well-regulated mind into tune, that I blush to make the comparison. Yet I sigh to think how few women try to attain this respectability by withdrawing from the giddy whirl of pleasure, or from the idle calm that stupefies the good sort of women it draws in.

Proud of their weakness, however, they must always be protected, shielded from care and from all the hard labour that dignifies the mind. If this is the decree of fate, if they choose to make themselves insignificant and contemptible, to sweetly waste “life away,” then let them not expect to be valued when their beauty fades; for it is the fate of the fairest flowers to be admired and then pulled to pieces by the careless hand that plucked them. In how many ways, out of the purest benevolence, do I wish to press this truth upon my sex! Yet I fear they will not listen to a truth that hard-won experience has brought home to many a troubled heart, nor willingly give up the privileges of rank and sex for the privileges of humanity, to which those who do not carry out its duties have no claim.

In my opinion, those writers are especially useful who make man feel for man, regardless of the station he fills or the trappings of artificial sentiment. So I would gladly convince reasonable men of the importance of some of my remarks, and persuade them to weigh the whole drift of my observations without passion. I appeal to their understanding; and, as a fellow creature, I claim in the name of my sex some place in their hearts. I beg them to help set their companion free, to make her a help meet for them!

If men would only generously snap our chains, and be content with rational companionship instead of slavish obedience, they would find us more attentive daughters, more affectionate sisters, more faithful wives, more reasonable mothers — in a word, better citizens. We should then love them with true affection, because we should learn to respect ourselves; and the peace of mind of a worthy man would not be disturbed by his wife’s idle vanity, nor would his babies be sent to nestle at a stranger’s breast, never having found a home at their mother’s.
